role: Obstruction Clearance Inspector at Tianfu Airport
headline: A civil aviation vocational graduate who mowed grass and patrolled pavement at the old airport, transferred to Jianyang the year the new airport opened, and now drives a patrol truck between rice paddies and new-town construction sites measuring tower cranes and chasing kites
unit: The obstruction clearance team of the airfield services department, Chengdu Tianfu International Airport
education: Vocational college diploma in airport operations and services
level: You can recite the layers of obstacle limitation surfaces on the clearance chart, you get a reading on a crane top with RTK in under ten minutes, and you have your own way of talking kite flyers down. But when it comes to sitting across from a site manager or township officials to negotiate cutting something down, you don't yet carry weight, and writing obstacle assessments isn't your job yet.
intro: You went to a civil aviation vocational college in Guanghan, joined the airport group after graduating, and spent two years mowing grass and patrolling pavement at the old airport. The year the new airport opened in Jianyang, you were moved onto the clearance team. As of today, across the dozens of kilometers of paddies, hillsides and new-town construction sites off both ends of the runways, anything that pokes up above the limitation surfaces is your business.
salary_note: Estimate: airfield services posts at the Chengdu airport group are paid on the state-enterprise scale, with night-shift and fieldwork allowances, full social insurance and a housing fund, a little above the national average. Income is steady and rises slowly, one grade at a time.

facts.label: Airport Obstruction Clearance Inspector (current level)
facts.value: 2-4 years, ¥5,780–8,500 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Spotting someone flying a kite or drone in the clearance zone, talking them down on the spot and reporting it

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Completing a full clearance patrol route and filling in the record

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related listings nationwide, 0 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: You come down from the staff dorm and check the patrol truck with Old Feng: radios, the RTK receiver, binoculars, a roll of warning tape, a stack of clearance-protection leaflets. It isn't fully light yet, and the runway lights are on in rows.

You drive the country roads along the northern approach, freshly planted paddies on both sides and a new resettlement estate in the distance. You spot a tower crane you haven't seen before, stop, and note its coordinates and number.

You carry the RTK into the site and measure the elevation of the crane's top. Checked against the clearance chart, it's more than three meters over. The site manager says the district approved it. You ask to see the clearance review opinion; the height limit on it falls well short of his crane.

Passing a village entrance, you find a few households burning straw on the drying ground, the smoke drifting toward the runway. You get out and talk with an old man for ages. He says they've burned it this way for decades. In the end he douses it with a bucket of water.
Lunch is tofu pudding and rice at a little place in the township. Old Feng says wait till spring: the first clear day, the whole hillside will be full of kites.

The airport operations center comes over the radio: a flight crew has reported an unidentified object aloft east of the runway. You floor it and find two kids flying a kite on the riverbank with more than two hundred meters of line out. You help them reel it in, take photos and call the police station to log it.

Back at the office, the satellite-image comparison in the clearance system has flagged six changes. You go through them: two are new vegetable greenhouses, and one is a communications pole someone has put up on a hillside. That's for tomorrow, on site.

On the night shift you stand on the roof of the airfield services building looking out. Far off, a small red dot is drifting slowly upward: a sky lantern. You grab the radio and head that way with Old Feng.

ladder.title: Airfield Services Worker (clearance patrol)
ladder.focus: Patrol the clearance protection zone with the shift, record obstacles and objects aloft, and learn the regulations and the clearance chart.

ladder.title: Airport Obstruction Clearance Inspector
ladder.focus: Patrol on your own, measure and verify new obstacles, deal with drones, kites and other objects aloft, and report them.

ladder.title: Obstruction Clearance Specialist
ladder.focus: Manage the obstacle register, coordinate with local government and police on removals, and take part in clearance assessments.

ladder.title: Airfield Services / Airside Operations Supervisor
ladder.focus: Oversee the clearance, electromagnetic environment and airside patrol teams.

ladder.title: Head of Clearance and Electromagnetic Environment Management
ladder.focus: Draw up the airport's clearance protection rules and work with the civil aviation authority and local government.

ai_tasks.name: Completing a full clearance patrol route and filling in the record
ai_tasks.how: AI can compare satellite imagery, drone photos and the last patrol's pictures, flag new buildings, cranes and suspicious changes automatically, and help organize the record and draft the report. A person still has to go and confirm on site, judge which changes are really a risk, and answer for what gets reported.

ai_tasks.name: Checking whether a tower crane on a new construction project is too tall
ai_tasks.how: AI can take the coordinates and elevation data, check them against the obstacle limitation surfaces, estimate how far over it is and draft a rectification notice. A person has to remeasure on site with instruments, verify the data, negotiate face to face with the site and the developer, and make the final call.

ai_tasks.name: Spotting someone flying a kite or drone in the clearance zone, talking them down on the spot and reporting it
ai_tasks.how: AI or detection equipment can help find objects aloft and give a location. But getting there, talking to the person flying, gathering evidence and reporting to the police all have to be done by a person, and if there's a confrontation, a person answers for it.

ai_tasks.name: Verifying and handling an unidentified object aloft after the operations center restricts flights
ai_tasks.how: AI can pull together radar, cameras, crew reports and drone detection, quickly narrow down the likely source and location, and assemble a timeline. Under time pressure a person has to go verify on site, coordinate with air traffic control, the operations center and the police, and decide what to do and whether to lift the restriction.

ai_tasks.name: Giving clearance-protection talks at nearby schools and communities
ai_tasks.how: AI can generate the copy, posters, slides and versions aimed at children or the elderly. A person has to go to the schools and neighborhoods, talk face to face and answer questions, and rely on trust and presence to make the rules stick.

ai_tasks.name: Reviewing the annual obstacle register and supporting the clearance assessment
ai_tasks.how: AI can check the register against survey data and find entries that are missing, duplicated or show odd changes in height, and compile the assessment material. A person has to check on site that obstruction lights and markings work, remeasure heights, sign for the register's accuracy and work with the assessors.

events.e_kongming: On Mid-Autumn night, several villages around the airport release dozens of sky lanterns at once, drifting toward the approach path. Your whole team runs between six villages all night, and when you get back it's daylight and your shoes are caked in mud.
events.e_crane_save: One night you find a tower crane in the new town with its obstruction light off and two meters over the limit. You phone the site manager out of bed, and the crane drops a section that same night. Two weeks later the civil aviation inspectors come, and that's exactly the area they check.
events.e_film: A gale tears the plastic sheeting off nearby greenhouses and lifts it into the sky, and one piece snags on a frame of the approach lights. You and Old Feng spend half an hour reaching for it with long poles before you get it down, and your hand gets a cut.
events.e_balloon: A village is holding a wedding and plans to release a hundred helium balloons during the ceremony. You call on them the day before and talk with the groom's family for an hour. In the end the balloons are tied to the arch instead, and they insist you drink a cup of wedding wine.
events.e_spotter: On a weekend a few aviation fans fly a drone on the extended runway centerline to film landings, and the detection system goes off. You get there and they say they're flying very low. You show them the limitation surfaces, they pack the drone up, and ask if you can tell them somewhere they're allowed to shoot.
events.e_flight_hold: One evening a crew reports an unidentified drone on the approach. Two flights go around and the ones behind hold in the air for twenty minutes. You search for an hour and never find the operator. At the meeting the next day, you draw every route you took in that hour, line by line.
events.e_scolded: A contractor hears you're going to report his crane as too tall and jabs a finger at you for ten minutes, saying a day's stoppage costs him tens of thousands. You don't answer back. You hand him the measurements and the limitation surface chart, and the next day the crane comes down.
events.e_summer: July in Jianyang, thirty-eight degrees, and you're on a treeless hillside with the RTK on your back measuring a newly raised utility pole. Sweat soaks through your work clothes twice, and back in the truck you drain a whole bottle of water.
events.e_rain_stuck: After a night of rain your patrol truck sinks into the mud on a path between paddies. A villager nearby comes with his tractor to pull you out, and afterward he says: you're the ones who come round every day about the kites, aren't you.
events.e_satellite: The clearance system is hooked up to automatic comparison of satellite and aerial imagery. Every morning when you switch on, the new buildings, cranes and suspicious changes are already circled. You no longer have to search road by road, but you still drive out to see every red circle with your own eyes.
events.e_ai_false: In one week the system throws more than twenty height warnings. You check each on site, and over a dozen turn out to be shadows in the imagery and quilts airing on rooftops. Back at the office you label each false alarm one by one and write them into the rules.
events.e_detect: The airport installs a drone detection and location system, and the screen shows roughly where the operator is. The first time you follow its fix, you find a middle-school boy on the roof of an apartment block. He's so scared he hides the controller behind his back.
events.e_school: You give a talk on clearance protection at a nearby primary school, bringing a kite and a clearance chart. Afterward a little boy raises his hand and asks how high his kite can fly. You say it can fly, but only somewhere far away from the airport.
events.e_laser: A crew reports being hit by a laser on approach. You and an officer from the police station keep watch for three nights and find, high up in a new apartment block, someone teasing a cat with a laser pointer who had no idea there was a flight path outside the window.
events.e_snake: Measuring the height of a big tree in a patch of wild grass, you hear a rustle by your feet as a rat snake slides past. You freeze for a few seconds, wait until it's gone, and finish taking the reading.
events.e_audit: Civil aviation auditors come for an operational safety audit, and one points at a random obstacle in the register and asks to see it on site. You drive him forty minutes to a hilltop. That tree was cut down to height last year, and you even pull up the photos from the day.
events.e_cert: You pass the senior-grade certificate for civil airport airfield services workers. The practical exam has you judge from a chart whether an obstacle exceeds the limits and how to report it, and your answer is more detailed than the model answer.
events.e_wedding: You get married, to someone who works ground services in the terminal. The wedding is in Jianyang town, and you make a point of telling the wedding company: no balloons, no fireworks. The emcee laughs and says you airport people really are particular.
events.e_house: You buy an apartment in the Eastern New Area with windows facing the approach path. On sleepless nights you count the planes coming down one after another, lights on, and by the seventh you're asleep.
events.e_child: Your child is born. On weekends you fly a kite with your child below your building, letting out only twenty meters of line. The neighbors laugh; you say it's an occupational habit.
events.e_newtown: The Eastern New Area's buildings get taller every year, and your register grows from three hundred-odd entries to more than a thousand. You put a big map on the office wall and add a pin for each new obstacle. The wall is nearly full.
events.e_knees: After twenty years of climbing hillsides and walking paddy banks, your knees start hurting on the way down. You hand the hilltop climbs to the young ones and watch them take readings through binoculars from the bottom.
events.e_lowalt: Low-altitude flying grows every year: delivery drones, sightseeing helicopters, crop-spraying aircraft over the fields, all of them routed around the airport. At a meeting you realize that what you look after is no longer just things growing up out of the ground.

c_drone.title: Get a drone license and learn aerial inspection
c_drone.situation: The team wants to try using drones to inspect hilltops and construction sites, far faster than driving, but it's short of licensed pilots. The civil drone operator license means two weeks of classes in Chengdu and weekend practice, and once you have it, the inspections, modeling and comparisons will all fall to you.

options.label: Take the exam and learn to fly
options.result: You get the license, and the first time you fly over the Longquan Mountains and look down, the limitation surfaces off both runway ends appear on the screen, for the first time, as something solid. From then on you fly all the team's aerial work.

options.label: Skip it and stay on the ground
options.result: You say your legs are more reliable than a drone. The license goes to a new young colleague, and you spend six months on the ground with him, showing him which tree and which pole you can't make out from the air.

c_specialist.title: Take over the obstacle register and go for Obstruction Clearance Specialist
c_specialist.situation: Your team leader wants you to take over the entire obstacle register: more than a thousand entries, each needing coordinates, elevation, a handling record and photos, plus liaising with the district, the townships and the police and staying on top of every illegal structure that has to be cut down or removed. Do it and you become an Obstruction Clearance Specialist. It also means half your time in the office on the phone and writing official letters.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You spend six months checking the register from start to finish, deleting dozens of entries for things long since demolished and adding over a hundred that were never logged. At your first coordination meeting at the district, you lay the material on the table, and nobody says the airport is making a fuss anymore.

options.label: You'd rather stay in the field
options.result: The register goes to another colleague. You keep driving the patrol truck out, and whenever anyone on the team needs to find an obstacle, you're still the first person they ask.

c_deadline.title: A district priority project is racing a deadline
c_deadline.situation: Two tower cranes on a priority project in the new town are over the limitation surface, but the project manager says they're due to top out next month, the district is on them every day, and if they stop for a single day the whole city will hear about it. You can report it right away and have them stop and lower the cranes, or give them two days and watch them yourself while they lower the cranes overnight.

options.label: Report it right away
options.result: The project stops for three days. A district official phones your department to ask who reported it. Your department head says one of ours did, by the rules, and nothing more comes of it.

options.label: Give them two days and watch
options.result: You spend both nights crouched at the edge of the site watching them take the two cranes down section by section. Early on the third morning you submit the after-lowering data. The project manager sends you a text every holiday after that.

c_home.title: The regional airport back home
c_home.situation: The regional airport in your hometown of Nanchong is hiring an airfield services supervisor to run clearance, bird control and pavement, and it badly needs someone from a big airport. A quarter less pay, but your parents would be half an hour away, and there your word would carry.

options.label: Go back to Nanchong
options.result: The regional airport has a dozen-odd flights a day, and you run the whole operation yourself, signing for everything from bird-scaring cannons to pavement cracks. On weekends you go home for dinner, and your mother says you've put on weight.

options.label: Stay at Tianfu
options.result: You don't leave. Tianfu's flights grow day by day, and the new town you look after grows taller. At New Year your father asks how big the airport in Chengdu is. You say it takes an hour to drive around it.

c_ai.title: Set the rules for AI-assisted patrols
c_ai.situation: Satellite comparison, aerial recognition and drone detection are all running now, producing dozens of warnings a day. The department wants someone to set the rules: which warnings need a person on site, which can be closed directly, how false alarms are labeled, how the rules get revised. It's office work, and it isn't on any performance sheet.

options.label: Take it and set the rules
options.result: You dig out three years of false alarms and sort them one by one, then set an order for what to check first and what next. Six months later, the sites your team has to visit each day drop from twenty-odd to seven or eight, and every one of them is real.

options.label: Decline and keep patrolling
options.result: You say you still trust your own eyes. The IT department writes the rules; you read them and add a few at the meeting: don't trust imagery from the day after rain; quilts on rooftops get mistaken for water tanks.

c_lowalt.title: A low-altitude monitoring platform wants you
c_lowalt.situation: A company has been set up in the Eastern New Area to run low-altitude connected air traffic, managing drone routes and a low-altitude monitoring platform. It's hiring a system administrator and likes that you understand clearance and can fly drones. Over twenty percent more pay, an office job, no more chasing kites. But you'd be leaving the airport.

options.label: Go to the low-altitude platform
options.result: You hand the patrol truck keys to your team leader and drive one last lap around the runways.
options.end: You go to the low-altitude platform, and from then on what you watch is drone routes, line after line on a screen. Every time you see the red no-fly ring around the airport, you know which paddy, which hilltop and which tower crane lie behind that line.

options.label: Stay at the airport
options.result: You turn it down. That week you take in three more kites on the riverbank, one from a child you'd talked to before. He sees you coming and reels in the line himself.

c_supervisor.title: Apply for Airfield Services / Airside Operations Supervisor
c_supervisor.situation: The department is promoting an Airfield Services / Airside Operations Supervisor to oversee the clearance, electromagnetic environment and airside patrol teams: dozens of people, rosters, emergency command, daily meetings with air traffic control and the operations center. If you get it, you'll rarely take a patrol truck out yourself again.

options.label: Apply
options.result: At the interview you skip the big speeches and talk about the day two flights went around and you searched an hour without finding anyone, and the three things you changed afterward. The old director on the panel nods.

options.label: Stay on the front line
options.result: You recommend a colleague and stay on as the backbone of the clearance team. New recruits all want to ride in your truck; they say a day out with you is worth more than a month of reading regulations.

c_planning.title: The administrative committee wants you for planning review
c_planning.situation: The Eastern New Area's administrative committee is hiring an airport planning and construction officer who understands clearance, to pre-review every new project around the airport and stop over-height buildings while they're still drawings. It's an office job with regular hours, but you'd be leaving the airport group for another organization.

options.label: Go to the committee
options.result: You photograph the pin-covered map on the wall and leave it for whoever takes over.
options.end: You do clearance pre-review at the committee for many years, and drawing after drawing comes out of your hands a few meters shorter. Every time you pass the neat, level rooftops of the new town, you know why they stop at that height.

options.label: Stay at the airport
options.result: You say you want to see it through at the airport. The committee hires someone else, and for every drawing that person isn't sure about, they phone you first.

c_head.title: Go for Head of Clearance and Electromagnetic Environment Management
c_head.situation: The airport is revising its clearance protection rules and has to deal with more and more low-altitude flying and electromagnetic interference. It wants a Head of Clearance and Electromagnetic Environment Management in the department, to work with civil aviation and local government and sign every assessment opinion. Every word you sign, you'll answer for if something goes wrong.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: At the review you bring out twenty years of register curves: cranes, kites, drones, sky lanterns, how many of each every year. The vice president in charge looks them over and says: this person knows what's what.

options.label: Don't apply; lead the team well
options.result: You say you'd rather stay in the airfield services building. The new head transfers in from another airport, and for his first month he asks you out on patrol every day. You take him to every hilltop.

endings.retire: On your last day you drive one more lap around the runways in the patrol truck. The truck is new; the route is the same. You stop at the far end of the northern approach lights and watch a plane come down low over your head, gear down, lights blinking. Back at the airfield services building, you set your radio on the desk.
endings.burnout: That year your knees and your back both give out, and the doctor says no more climbing hilltops or walking paddy banks. The department moves you to the records room to sort twenty years of clearance registers and photos. You leave on time every day, and on the way home you still look up at the sky for a small red dot that shouldn't be there.

stages: You drive your route through the clearance protection zone in the patrol truck, carry the RTK to measure the new cranes, poles and big trees, and judge on the clearance chart whether they're over the limit. When the operations center reports something aloft, you head that way, talk kite flyers, drone pilots and lantern releasers into stopping, photograph the evidence and notify the police station. You fill in the patrol records yourself; assessments and official letters are still signed by the team leader.

What you manage now is the whole obstacle register: more than a thousand coordinates, elevations and handling records, every one of which has to match the ground. You write letters to the district and townships, sit in coordination meetings with housing, planning and site owners negotiating cuts and removals item by item, and when civil aviation comes to audit, you take them up the hills with the register and the photos. You drive out less, and spend more time on the phone and in meetings.

You oversee the clearance, electromagnetic environment and airside patrol teams, and the rosters, emergency plans and quarterly drills for dozens of people are in your hands. Every day you meet with air traffic control and the operations center, and when something unidentified goes up, you dispatch people and trucks from the command room. What you sign has changed from patrol records to assessment opinions and rectification notices.

You decide how the airport's clearance protection rules are revised and how low-altitude flying and the electromagnetic environment are managed. You work with the civil aviation authority, local government and the low-altitude monitoring platform, and speak for the airport at the new town's planning reviews; the last page of every clearance assessment carries your name. When you go out, it's to see the one obstacle hardest to deal with.
work: Old Feng sends you alone to measure a new signal tower at the foot of the Longquan Mountains. You set up the RTK, take three readings and average them: a meter twenty under the limitation surface. You write the number in the log and photograph it from four directions.

An old man who keeps pigeons lets them out every afternoon, and the flock circles right across the approach. You call on him three times, and on the third you bring a chart of the flight path. He agrees to let them out in the morning instead, when there are fewer flights.
The satellite comparison flags a new white spot on a hillside. You drive forty minutes to find a family's new solar water heater on their roof, not over the limit, and close it out in the system.

You write to a township government asking for the removal of three over-height eucalyptus trees on a hilltop, attaching the measurements and the limitation surface chart. A township official comes with you to see the owner, and in the end you settle on topping them rather than cutting them down.

One obstacle in the register hasn't been remeasured in ten years. You take a young colleague up to measure it again and find the building has since added a floor; it's four meters taller than the old record.

At a coordination meeting a developer's representative says his building is only a meter over, no big deal. You don't argue. You spread out an approach profile for a flight and show him where that meter sits relative to the plane.

Before Spring Festival you draw up two weeks of special patrol rosters with someone posted at every village entrance. On New Year's Eve you sit in the command room as one radio after another reports all clear, and only go back to the dorm after midnight.

An unidentified drone restricts flights, and from the command room you dispatch three trucks and two detection points. In forty minutes you find the operator, and ten minutes later you call the operations center: clear to lift.

The first time a new airfield services worker tries to talk down a kite flyer, she gets shouted at and cries. You say nothing. The next day you drive her out yourself and have her stand beside you to watch how you say the first sentence.

For the revision of the airport's clearance protection rules, you and a few colleagues go back through twenty years of handling records and write sky lanterns, helium balloons and laser pointers into the clauses, each one backed by something that really happened.
At a new-town planning review, the design for a landmark tower is twenty meters above the limitation surface. You speak for ten minutes, and in the end the design becomes two shorter buildings.

You and the low-altitude platform team draw the low-altitude routes around the airport. They want delivery drones to skim along the limitation surfaces; you push the line five hundred meters out on the chart and sign it.
past: You go to middle school in the countryside outside Nanchong. Now and then a plane draws a white line across the sky over the village, and you lie on a haystack watching it slowly fade.

Your gaokao (college entrance exam) score isn't high. Leafing through the admissions catalog you find a civil aviation vocational college in Guanghan, figure that at least it's near planes, and apply for airport operations and services.

In your second year you intern at the old airport, mowing grass, patrolling pavement and picking up foreign objects with the airfield services crew. The first time you watch a wide-body land from beside the runway, its tires throw up a puff of white smoke, and your ears ring for ages.

After graduation you pass the exam into the airport group as an airfield services worker. Every night after the last flight, you walk the runway meter by meter with your mentor and a flashlight, looking for a single screw, a single pebble.

The new airport opens in Jianyang and airfield services is forming a clearance team, so you sign up. Old Feng, who patrolled clearance at the old airport for twenty years, presses a dog-eared clearance chart into your hands on the first day.

late.pension_note: Estimate: the airport group is state-owned and pays full pension contributions on actual wages, plus a company annuity. Together they come to a little over half your last monthly pay.
scenes: In your first month of retirement you still wake at 6:30 and reach for the radio on the nightstand. Your hand finds the phone instead. The forecast says sunny, windy. You think: there'll be more kites on the hillsides today.
The airport invites you back to teach new airfield services workers. You don't use slides. You drive them along the old route and tell a story from back then at every junction.
You plant a few pomelo trees in the yard back home, and when you prune them you can't help keeping them to a certain height. A neighbor asks why you won't let them grow. You say it's a habit.

Your grandchild wants to fly a kite, and you take him to a riverbank far from the airport and let the line run all the way out. He asks: Grandpa, didn't you used to stop people flying kites? You say that was somewhere else.
The records room is quiet. You scan twenty years of clearance photos into the system one by one, and when you come to one of Old Feng's back as he measures a crane, you stop and look for a long time.

Once you stop climbing hilltops, your knees slowly get a little better. In the evenings you walk around the compound and look up at the planes coming down, one after another, and go home at the seventh.
On the day you file your retirement papers you hand the dog-eared clearance chart back to the department. The team leader says keep it as a souvenir, but you leave it on the desk anyway.

In your first year away from the airport, whenever you see a small red dot in the sky your hand goes to your belt. There's no radio there, and only then do you remember it isn't yours to deal with anymore.
Back at the airport on an errand, you see a row of new patrol trucks outside the airfield services building, with a logo you've never seen. A young man jumps down from one with an RTK on his back.
The airfield services worker you trained has become a supervisor. She sends you a photo: the big map on the team's wall has been replaced with a new one, the pins even denser.

Another stretch of new buildings goes up in the Eastern New Area. Driving past, you can tell at a glance which ones stopped at the limitation surface; their rooftops are as level as if drawn with a ruler.
In an old box you find your first patrol log. On page one, in your shaky handwriting, are the coordinates of a tower crane, followed by: three point two meters over, notified.

closing.retire: Many years later, one evening, you sit halfway up a slope of the Longquan Mountains watching the airport's lights come on in lines, as a plane comes down from high above you. The sky is clean, with nothing in it but the plane.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you are watering plants on the balcony when a very small kite drifts across the sky, far away and low. You watch it a while and think it's flying at just the right height.
closing.end: Many years later, in a drawer, you find the dog-eared clearance chart, the lines of its limitation surfaces faded. You spread it out on the table and trace a finger slowly along the runway's direction, then roll it up and put it back.
